metadata.title: Orbit Faster to Go Slower
metadata.register: formal, undergrad/grad audience, no casual narration
metadata.branding: none — unbranded, book content only, no channel/logo/handle

beats.narration_text: Fire a satellite's engine forward to speed it up. Why does it end up moving slower?
beats.new_visual_element: Portrait-only opening question card (title-styled, crimson underline).

beats.narration_text: A satellite circles Earth. Fire its engine forward, along its direction of motion, and it gains speed. Yet once it settles into its new circular orbit, that orbit is higher, and the satellite is moving more slowly than before. How can speeding up leave it slower?
beats.new_visual_element: Earth (blue with teal land), a dashed circular orbit, a satellite (gold body, slate panels) moving counterclockwise to the top with an ink velocity arrow v1. A crimson forward-thrust arrow flashes beside it; the orbit grows to a larger circle and the velocity arrow shortens to v2 < v1.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: Earth, larger orbit, satellite at top, shorter velocity arrow labeled v2 < v1, faint original orbit

beats.narration_text: For a circular orbit, gravity supplies exactly the centripetal force, and that fixes the kinetic energy: K equals G M m over two r. The potential energy is minus G M m over r. So the total energy is minus G M m over two r. It is negative, and it is exactly the negative of the kinetic energy.
beats.new_visual_element: Back at the original orbit. Equation slot: K = GMm/2r, then U = -GMm/r, then E = -GMm/2r = -K. Horizontal energy bars on a number line with a zero mark: K (teal, positive), U (crimson, twice as long, negative), E (ink, negative, same length as K).
beats.accumulated_scene_state: orbit r1 with satellite and v1, final equation E = -GMm/2r = -K, three energy bars

beats.narration_text: A forward burn adds energy, so E becomes less negative. Since E is minus G M m over two r, a less negative E means a larger r. And because the kinetic energy equals minus E, a larger orbit has less kinetic energy. The satellite ends up higher and slower.
beats.new_visual_element: Thrust arrow flashes; one tracker drives everything: the E bar shrinks toward zero, the orbit grows, the K bar shortens, the U bar shortens, and the velocity arrow shortens.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: larger orbit, shorter v arrow, E bar nearer zero, K bar shorter

beats.narration_text: Braking does the opposite. A backward burn removes energy, E becomes more negative, the orbit shrinks, and the kinetic energy grows. The satellite drops lower and ends up moving faster.
beats.new_visual_element: Return to the original orbit. Crimson thrust arrow now points backward; the orbit shrinks to a smaller circle, the E bar grows more negative, the K bar grows, and the velocity arrow lengthens to v3 > v1.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: smaller orbit, longer v arrow, E bar more negative, K bar longer

beats.narration_text: Total energy and orbital speed move in opposite directions. Less energy means a tighter, faster orbit, and more energy means a wider, slower one. In orbit, braking is how you speed up.
beats.new_visual_element: Final frame: the larger dashed orbit labeled 'higher: more E, slower' and the smaller orbit with the satellite labeled 'lower: less E, faster'; equation E = -GMm/2r = -K stays on screen.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: final held frame with both orbits labeled and the equation
